It prevents a hiatus. fr.Wiktionary treats -ter as a variant of -er; en.Wiktionary treats the -t- as euphonic. The sources do not state a fixed rule for when it is inserted.
-t-.origin_en: Not an affix of its own: ~-t-~ is an epenthetic consonant inserted before the verbal ending ~-er~, which comes from Latin ~-are~.
-t-.origin_fr: Ce n'est pas un affixe à part : ~-t-~ est une consonne épenthétique insérée devant la terminaison verbale ~-er~, qui vient du latin ~-are~.
senses: no meaning of its own; the sense is that of -er (denominal: 'provide with N', 'work on N'): biseauter 'cut at a bevel', clouter 'stud with nails'
with a prefix as well: dénoyauter, dépiauter (dé- + noun + -t-er) 'remove N'
-t-.productive: Productive as a variant of -er, mostly for denominal verbs in informal or technical registers (yoyoter, queuter, réseauter).
cognates: No cognate affix: it is a feature of French phonology
-t-.pitfalls: Do not call -t- a suffix with a meaning. Most app verbs ending in -ter have a t that belongs to the root, so there is no -ter affix: rester (Latin restare), présenter, porter, ajouter, éviter, limiter, traiter (Latin tractare), accepter, contacter, adapter, acheter, adopter, hésiter, visiter, nécessiter, quitter, compter (Latin computare), monter, écouter, raconter. A true -t- verb needs: (1) a noun or word base that ends in a vowel (clou, biseau, queue, yoyo, noyau); (2) that base exists in French independently; (3) a verb without the t would be a different or non-existing word or would have a hiatus (clouer exists as 'nail', clouter as 'stud', so check sense); (4) no Latin ancestor. dépiauter shows a Picard base piau (a form of peau) + epenthetic -t-. Where the base noun itself ends in t (e.g., a noun like 'rapport'), the t belongs to the noun and is not epenthetic. The evidence words the same pattern differently: biseauter is given as 'biseau + -ter', clouter as 'clou + -t- + -er'; both describe the same epenthetic t.

-iser.allomorphy: -iser is the only form that forms French verbs. The group lists -ise, but fr.Wiktionary gives -ise only as the British English counterpart of -ize, so treat it as the same suffix without its infinitive ending, not as a second French verb suffix. A separate noun suffix -ise (bêtise, franchise) is a different affix and gives no verbs. The stem often changes before -iser: final -el, -al or -ique may be dropped or reshaped (réel to réaliser, numérique to numériser, informatique to informatiser, automate to automatiser).
-iser.origin_en: Borrowed into Old French as ~-iser~ (earlier ~-izer~) from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. fr.Wiktionary instead dates its productive use to the mid-sixteenth century (~latiniser~, ~gréciser~).
-iser.origin_fr: Emprunté en ancien français sous la forme ~-iser~ (d'abord ~-izer~) au latin tardif ~-izāre~, qui transcrivait des verbes grecs. Le Wiktionnaire en date plutôt l'emploi productif du milieu du XVIᵉ siècle (~latiniser~, ~gréciser~).
senses: make or render A (moderniser, actualiser, concrétiser)
cause to become, convert into N (numériser, carboniser)
treat with, subject to N or to a person's or place's name (pasteuriser, galvaniser)
provide with N (informatiser, hospitaliser)
-iser.productive: Fully productive, in technical, administrative and journalistic registers (informatiser, numériser, dollariser, sarkozyser in fr.Wiktionary).
cognates: English -ize/-ise (same Late Latin and Greek source, reached English through French and Latin)
French -oyer (en.Wiktionary: -iser is a doublet of the inherited -oyer)
-iser.pitfalls: Many verbs in -iser are not formed in French from a base + -iser; they were borrowed whole from Latin or Greek: baptiser (Late Latin baptizare), civiliser (check the entry), organiser. In some verbs the -is- belongs to the root and the verb ends in -er, not -iser: croiser (croix + -er), diviser and réviser (Latin divisare, revisere), épuiser, apaiser (a- + paix), déguiser (dé- + guise), préciser (précis + -er), maîtriser, favoriser (favori), autoriser. Do not split these as X + -iser. Réaliser is a genuine -iser formation (réel + -iser with stem change per fr.Wiktionary), but an older sense of 'realize' may come through English; check. Before writing base + -iser, check that (a) the base is an existing French noun or adjective, with the stem change if any (réel/réal-, numérique/numér-), (b) the sense is 'make A', 'convert into N' or 'treat with N', (c) the entry is not marked as borrowed from Latin or Greek. Prefixed verbs such as décentraliser are dé- + centraliser, not dé- + central + -iser.

-ifier.allomorphy: -ifier is the usual form; -fier is the older variant. fr.Wiktionary (as summarized) says -fier was historically used when the stem already ended in -i or with Latin stems in -fico/-ficare (putréfier, liquéfier, stupéfier), while -ifier spread because French was used to the -i- of Latin compounds (-ificare). Today -ifier is much more common; -fier is used for a few later coinages (nazifier, zombifier, wikifier). The stem often changes: a noun or adjective loses its final vowel or letters (complexe + -ifier, intense + -ifier, authentique -> authentifier, personne -> personnifier).
-ifier.origin_en: From Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, which goes back to ~facere~ (“to make”).
-ifier.origin_fr: Du latin ~-(i)ficāre~, qui remonte à ~facere~ (« faire »).
senses: to make A, to render adjective-like (complexifier 'make complex', intensifier, densifier, fluidifier, humidifier)
to turn into or put in the form of N (plastifier, codifier 'put into a code', stratifier, personnifier)
to organize or treat according to N (planifier 'organize by a plan', classifier)
-ifier.productive: Productive: new verbs are still coined in learned, technical and journalistic registers (complexifier, planifier, authentifier). Some are also calques of English -ify (codifier, per fr.Wiktionary, may also come from English codify, attested 1800).
cognates: English -ify (from Old French -ifier, from Latin -ificare)
Italian -ificare and Spanish -ificar (same Latin source)
-ifier.pitfalls: Many app verbs ending in -ifier are inherited from Latin -ificare or borrowed from Latin already formed, with no French base: modifier, justifier, vérifier, signifier, sacrifier, qualifier, spécifier, certifier, notifier, amplifier, ratifier, édifier, rectifier, fortifier, purifier, glorifier, gratifier, fructifier, magnifier, sanctifier, crucifier, pacifier, terrifier, horrifier, béatifier, falsifier, identifier, simplifier, diversifier, clarifier, unifier, quantifier, ramifier. Check: if the Latin verb in -ficare exists, call it a Latin borrowing, not a French noun + -ifier. Verbs in -éfier (liquéfier, raréfier, putréfier) come from Latin -facere, via the -fier line, not from an -ifier derivation; the source distinguishes -fier from -ifier. Prefixed forms are prefix + an existing -ifier verb: disqualifier, requalifier, réunifier, démystifier. confier is NOT -ifier: it is con- + fier (Latin confidere), the -fi- is the root. clarifier, simplifier and similar may be Latin or French, so cite the Latin etymon when known.

-ier.allomorphy: No allomorphy: fr.Wiktionary describes domicilier's ending as the verbal suffix -er, en.Wiktionary writes domicile + -ier. Treat every verb on this card as base + the verb ending of the -er card. Do not trace it to the noun suffix -ier (Latin -ārius), which forms nouns such as argentier and does not form verbs.
-ier.origin_en: Not a verb suffix with a history of its own. In verbs such as ~domicilier~ (from ~domicile~) and ~pontifier~ (from ~pontife~), the ending is the ordinary verb ending ~-er~ after the base; the sources disagree only on what to call it. The noun suffix ~-ier~, from Latin ~-ārius~, is a different affix.
-ier.origin_fr: Pas un suffixe verbal doté d'une histoire propre. Dans des verbes comme ~domicilier~ (de ~domicile~) et ~pontifier~ (de ~pontife~), la terminaison est la désinence verbale ordinaire ~-er~ ajoutée à la base ; les sources ne divergent que sur son nom. Le suffixe nominal ~-ier~, du latin ~-ārius~, est un autre affixe.
senses: make or turn into N, act like N (pontifier, quintessencier)
provide with N, put in N (domicilier)
treat as or by means of N (holographier)
-ier.productive: Not a productive verb suffix. The handful of verbs the sources analyze this way (domicilier, pontifier, quintessencier, holographier) are isolated formations.
-ier.pitfalls: This card is dangerous to apply by default. The input list shows almost every app verb ending in -ier is not X + -ier. Many are Latin -ificare verbs in -ifier (modifier, identifier, vérifier, justifier, signifier, qualifier, simplifier, diversifier, certifier, spécifier, notifier, sacrifier, amplifier, planifier), where -ifier is the ending, not -ier. Many others are inherited or borrowed from Latin verbs in -iare or -icare: publier, oublier, étudier, associer, varier, apprécier, négocier, initier, envier, dédier, marier. relier and remercier are re- + lier and re- + merci + verb ending, and the -ier is part of the base. copier is from the noun copie. The sources say domicilier is from domicile and pontifier from pontife, and fr and en differ on how to name the suffix (fr calls it the verbal suffix -er, en calls it -ier). Say 'base noun + verb ending -ier' only for verbs whose base noun ends in -e or a consonant and which are not in the Latin lists above. Before writing noun + -ier, check that (a) the base is an existing French noun (domicile, pontife, quintessence), (b) the verb is not marked inherited or borrowed from Latin, (c) the ending is not -ifier.
-ier.skeptic: refuted; origin rewritten by the orchestrator from the skeptic's finding

-oyer.allomorphy: -oyer is the regular form after a stem (côtoyer, tournoyer); -ayer appears in a few verbs (balayer, bégayer) and -eyer is listed in fr.Wiktionary as a variant (the sources give no example here). -oyer is pronounced wa.je; fr.Wiktionary notes Littré recorded an [ɔ.je] pronunciation. In conjugation the -y- becomes -i- before a silent e (côtoie, tournoie); -ayer verbs may keep y or take i (balaie or balaye). tutoyer has an intercalary -t- (tu + -t- + -oyer).
-oyer.origin_en: From Old French ~-oiier~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~ (Vulgar Latin ~-idiare~ in one account); ~-iser~ is the learned doublet.
-oyer.origin_fr: De l'ancien français ~-oiier~, issu du bas latin ~-izāre~ (du latin vulgaire ~-idiare~ dans une autre présentation) ; ~-iser~ en est le doublet savant.
senses: repeated or continuing action (tournoyer 'keep turning', louvoyer, larmoyer)
to be or behave like N, to emit N (flamboyer 'blaze', verdoyer 'be green', foudroyer, chatoyer, rougeoyer)
to treat or address with N, to apply N (tutoyer, vouvoyer, côtoyer 'go along the côte', apitoyer 'move to pity')
-oyer.productive: Not productive for new verbs today. The ending exists in older verbs; modern coinages use -iser. vouvoyer was made on the pattern of tutoyer (the sources do not give a date).
cognates: French -iser (doublet from the same Late Latin -izāre)
English -ize (from Latin -izāre via Greek)
-oyer.pitfalls: Do NOT assume every verb in -oyer or -ayer is a suffixed derivation. Many app verbs ending in -oyer, -ayer, -uyer owe the y to the Latin root, not to the suffix: envoyer, renvoyer, fourvoyer, dévoyer, convoyer (from voie via en-/con-), employer, déployer (Latin plicare), payer and its prefixed forms prépayer, repayer, surpayer, sous-payer (Latin pacare), essayer (from the noun essai), effrayer, enrayer, délayer, relayer, déblayer, remblayer, embrayer, débrayer, pagayer, monnayer (monnaie), nettoyer (net + -oyer, a true derivative), octroyer (Old French otroier), corroyer, zézayer. For each, the y-alternation is a conjugation fact, not proof that the suffix was added. Ondoyer (onde) and atermoyer (a- + terme) are real -oyer derivatives, not Latin-root verbs (standard French morphology). Check that the base noun or verb exists (côte, tourner, foudre, tu, flamme) and that the sense is repetition, emission or being like N. The sources disagree on the Latin source (-izāre vs -idiare); both are given. balayer is disputed: fr.Wiktionary gives balai or baler + -ayer, en.Wiktionary gives balai + -er.

-oter.allomorphy: -oter is the usual spelling (clignoter, tapoter, siffloter); -otter is the spelling of a closed set of verbs (baisotter, bouillotter, cachotter, frisotter, and, by their base noun, boulotter, grelotter, culotter, calotter, marcotter), and some verbs hesitate (couchoter or couchotter, dansoter or dansotter, mangeoter or mangeotter). The double t in -otter follows the base noun: nouns in -otte or some in -ot give -otter, nouns in -ote or -o give -oter (pelote/peloter, numéro/numéroter). The 1960s spelling-reform proposals would drop the double letter in the exceptions (TLFi). -ot is not a verb suffix; it is the diminutive suffix from which -oter was built (-ot + -er). The form -ot is listed only so that evidence naming the diminutive -ot (siffloter: « avec le suffixe diminutif -ot ») finds this card. It is not a verb suffix itself: it is the noun and adjective diminutive from which -oter was built with the verb ending -er.
-oter.origin_en: Inherited from Middle French ~-oter~, from Old French ~-oter~, itself built from ~-ot~ + ~-er~.
-oter.origin_fr: Hérité du moyen français ~-oter~, issu de l'ancien français ~-oter~, lui-même formé de ~-ot~ + ~-er~.
senses: diminutive: a small, light action (tapoter 'tap lightly', picoter 'prick repeatedly', chipoter)
frequentative: an action repeated in small bursts (clignoter, siffloter, toussoter, grignoter)
attenuative or pejorative, colloquial (vivoter 'live meagerly', traficoter)
denominal, on a noun (chevroter 'to quaver, to bleat', papilloter)
-oter.productive: Yes, in familiar register. The TLFi says -ot(t)er is 'vivant tout au long de l'histoire de la langue', especially in the 15th and 16th centuries, and cites traficoter (mid-20th century) as a recent creation; fr.Wiktionary flags the suffix as familiar.
cognates: No cognate affix is established by the sources consulted. French Wiktionary lists competing suffixes -ailler, -ocher and -eter in French.
-oter.pitfalls: The final letters -oter or -otter are NOT proof of this suffix. The TLFi (remark 1) names the false positives: verbs formed on a noun in -ot, -ote, -otte or -o with plain -er. (1) Noun in -ot + -er: pivoter (pivot), comploter (complot), raboter (rabot), saboter (sabot), ligoter (ligot), ergoter (ergot), grelotter (grelot), boulotter, boycotter (boycott). (2) Noun in -ote/-otte + -er: piloter (pilote), menotter (menotte), marcotter (marcotte), culotter, capoter (capote). (3) Noun in -o + -er: numéroter (numéro; English Wiktionary writes numéro + -oter, the TLFi counts it with the false positives), siroter (sirop). (4) Latin loans: annoter (adnotare), connoter (Medieval Latin connotare), sangloter (singultare). (5) Other origins: dénoter (dé- + noter), revoter (re- + voter), tricoter (Frankish), chuchoter (imitative), mijoter (dialectal), radoter (Old French), escamoter (Occitan), shooter (English), papoter (an onomatopoeic base + -oter, a true suffix case), barboter and caboter (uncertain). The true -oter verbs have a base verb and a diminutive or frequentative sense: clignoter (cligner), tapoter (taper), siffloter (siffler), toussoter (tousser), vivoter (vivre), picoter (piquer), grignoter (grigner), gigoter (giguer), clapoter (claper). Before writing 'X + -oter', check that X is a French verb (or an onomatopoeic base) and that the sense is 'a little, repeatedly'. If the base is a noun ending in -ot, -ote, -otte or -o, write 'noun + -er'.

-ailler.allomorphy: One form, -ailler [a.je], attached to a verb stem (crier → criailler) or, less often, a noun (mouche → mouchailler). The stem's ending is dropped: crier → cri-, discuter → discut-.
-ailler.origin_en: Either inherited from Latin ~-āculāre~ or built in French from the noun suffix ~-aille~ and the verbal ending ~-er~; the sources differ.
-ailler.origin_fr: Soit hérité du latin ~-āculāre~, soit formé en français à partir du suffixe nominal ~-aille~ et de la terminaison verbale ~-er~ ; les sources divergent.
senses: frequentative: repeated, petty action (tirailler, tournailler, traînailler)
pejorative: do badly or without conviction (discutailler, criticailler, couchailler, rimailler, criailler)
-ailler.productive: Productive for informal, often humorous or contemptuous coinages (disputailler, discutailler, criticailler).
cognates: No cognate in other languages is stated in the sources; none is claimed
-ailler.pitfalls: Many verbs ending in -ailler in the app are not 'verb + -ailler'. (1) Noun in -aille + -er: batailler (bataille), mitrailler (mitraille), ferrailler (ferraille), rempailler/empailler (paille), entailler (taille), détailler (taille), ravitailler/avitailler (vitaille). The -ailler here is -aille + -er, an accidental match. (2) Other nouns: dérailler (rail), médailler (médaille), cisailler (cisaille), tenailler (tenaille), gouailler, chamailler, pinailler. (3) travailler comes from Vulgar Latin *tripaliare, not -ailler. Derived forms with re- or dé- (retravailler, débroussailler, retailler, remailler) follow their base. Real -ailler verbs are ones whose base is a verb and whose sense is a pejorative frequentative: tirailler (tirer), criailler (crier), traînailler (traîner), discutailler, disputailler, écrivailler, sonnailler, tournailler. Check before writing: the base verb exists and the sense is 'do repeatedly or badly'. rimailler: fr.Wiktionary says 'de rimer avec le suffixe péjoratif -ailler' but en.Wiktionary says 'from rimaille + -er'; the sources differ. fr.Wiktionary treats the suffix as possibly inherited from Latin -aculare.

-asser.allomorphy: -asser is the verbal form. -asse is the stem of the same suffix before the infinitive ending: fr.Wiktionary gives -asse alongside -asser, and the evidence sample écrivasser says 'suffixe -asse'. The sample coupasser has -asser. Before the suffix the base loses its final vowel or ending (rêver to rêv-asser, écrire to écriv-asser, grogner to grogn-asser).
-asser.origin_en: A French suffix of the fifteenth century, formed from ~-ace~ and ~-asse~ with the verb ending ~-er~.
-asser.origin_fr: Suffixe français du XVᵉ siècle, formé à partir de ~-ace~ et de ~-asse~ avec la terminaison verbale ~-er~.
senses: pejorative or depreciative: do X badly or without result (rêvasser, écrivasser)
frequentative: repeat X (traînasser, grognasser)
diminutive: do X weakly or lightly (pleuvasser, brouillasser)
-asser.productive: Still productive in familiar speech, notably for weather verbs (pleuvasser, brouillasser) per fr.Wiktionary; fr.Wiktionary notes it is used especially in western France and Canada.
cognates: none given in the sources
-asser.pitfalls: Most app verbs that end in -asser are not base + -asser. fr.Wiktionary says outright that amasser, fracasser and ressasser have different etymologies. Many contain the base passer (dépasser, repasser, surpasser, outrepasser, trépasser, contre-passer: all prefix + passer, where the -asser is just the end of passer), classer (reclasser, déclasser, surclasser, interclasser) or chasser (pourchasser). Others are built on a noun ending in -ace/-asse: cuirasser (cuirasse), matelasser (matelas), cadenasser (cadenas), crevasser (crevasse), encrasser and décrasser (crasse), compasser (compas), terrasser (terrasse or terre; check), dégueulasser (dégueulasse). embrasser is en- + bras + -er; entasser is en- + tas + -er; ramasser is from amasser; délasser is dé- + las; prélasser comes from prélat. concasser is from Latin conquassare. harasser, tabasser, jacasser, croasser, fricasser: check. The genuine verbal ones, per fr.Wiktionary, are rêvasser, traînasser, tracasser, bavasser, paperasser, potasser, pleuvasser, brouillasser. fr.Wiktionary derives tracasser from traquer and potasser from potache, so the base is not always the obvious verb. Before writing verb + -asser, check that (a) the base is a French verb or noun that remains clearly present in the meaning, (b) the sense is pejorative, frequentative or diminutive, (c) the verb is not a prefix + passer, classer or chasser.

-eter.allomorphy: -eter is -et + -er (fr.Wiktionary). The -et- can also be read as a form inside the verb (haleter, from haler + -et-). Before a silent e the t is either doubled (jette-type: il cliquette, tachette) or the e opens to è (il halète, corsète); the 1990 reform extended the è type. Both patterns belong to the same suffix and do not change the sense.
-eter.origin_en: Formed in French from the suffixes ~-et~ and ~-er~.
-eter.origin_fr: Formé en français des suffixes ~-et~ et ~-er~.
senses: diminutive: do a little or on a small scale (tacheter 'mark with small spots', moucheter, pelleter)
frequentative: do repeatedly or in short bursts (cliqueter, haleter, becqueter)
no clear sense: a verb made from a noun (pailleter)
-eter.productive: Not productive today. Verbs in -eter are old; modern coinages use other patterns.
cognates: None firmly established in the sources used
-eter.pitfalls: Most -eter verbs are NOT 'base + -eter'. Three groups: (1) the stem is already a noun in -et and -er is simply added: feuilleter (feuillet), fureter (furet), fileter (filet), crocheter (crochet), colleter (collet), décolleter (dé- + collet + -er), cacheter (cachet), breveter (brevet), riveter (rivet), souffleter (soufflet), caqueter and hoqueter (onomatopoeia), étiqueter (étiquette), trompeter (trompette). (2) Inherited Latin: acheter (Vulgar Latin accaptare), and its prefixed forms racheter. (3) jeter-based: rejeter, projeter, interjeter, déjeter (jeter is from Latin iactare, not -eter). Conjugation (jette/achète) is a separate fact. A writer must check whether -et belongs to a noun (use 'noun in -et + -er') or is the suffix (tacheter, moucheter). The sources themselves disagree: haleter is haler + -et-; pelleter is pelle + -et + -er; becqueter is bec + -eter or becquer + -eter.

-eler.allomorphy: One suffix form, but the spelling of the stem is not uniform: some -eler verbs double the l before a mute e (il appelle, il bosselle, il ficelle) and others take è (il gèle, il cisèle, il modèle). The TLFi lists each verb as elle or èle (for instance èle in celer, congeler, déceler, dégeler, démanteler, écarteler, geler, marteler, modeler, peler, receler; elle in appeler, atteler, bosseler, chanceler, ensorceler, ficeler, jumeler, museler, niveler, renouveler, ruisseler). The spelling is a property of the verb and does not show whether the suffix is present.
-eler.origin_en: According to the TLFi, ~-eler~ either descends from the Latin suffix ~-illare~, which already had a diminutive sense (~titillare~, ~vacillare~), or was built secondarily in French on the noun suffixes ~-el~, ~-eau~ and ~-elle~.
-eler.origin_fr: Selon le TLFi, ~-eler~ est soit issu du suffixe latin ~-illare~, qui avait déjà une valeur diminutive (~titillare~, ~vacillare~), soit créé secondairement en français sur les suffixes nominaux ~-el~, ~-eau~ et ~-elle~.
senses: diminutive or frequentative on a verb: a small repeated action (craqueler 'crack finely')
on a noun in -eau, -el, -elle: 'form or provide with N' (bosseler 'former des bosses', denteler 'to indent, to notch'; the TLFi also lists agneler, botteler, cordeler, cuveler, amonceler)
-eler.productive: Very little. The TLFi says -eler is 'fort peu productif' and has been supplanted by other diminutive suffixes (-iller): sautiller replaced sauteler, ventiler replaced venteler.
cognates: Latin -illare (the likely source; TLFi), as in titillare and vacillare
Related French suffixes -iller, -ouiller, -ailler (fr.Wiktionary)
English -le in crackle (English Wiktionary compares craqueler)
-eler.pitfalls: Most verbs ending in -eler are NOT formed with this suffix. The TLFi lists homophonous endings: appeler (Latin appellare, learned), atteler (Latin *attelare), celer, chanceler (Latin cancellare), ensorceler, épeler, étinceler, geler. (1) Latin loans or inherited Latin verbs: appeler and rappeler, congeler, chanceler, atteler. (2) Verbs on a French verb celer or geler: déceler and receler (dé-/re- + celer), dégeler, surgeler (prefix + geler), dételer (dé- + atteler). Write 'prefix + verb', not '-eler'. (3) Verbs from another language: grommeler (Old French grumeler, from Middle Dutch grommelen, itself a frequentative), épeler (Frankish). (4) Verbs that are a noun in -eau, -el or -elle + plain -er, which the TLFi lists as type B of -eler but which English Wiktionary treats as noun + -er: niveler (niveau), jumeler (jumeau), morceler (morceau), museler (musel), ficeler (ficelle), marteler (martel), étinceler (étincelle), carreler (carrel), pommeler (pommel), amonceler (a- + moncel + -er), ciseler (Old French cisel), ensorceler (sorcier + -er, with dissimilation). Prefer 'noun + -er' here and mention the -eler family only as background. (5) Disputed or opaque: harceler (from herser, 'to harrow'), écarteler, démanteler (no etymology given). The cleanest -eler cases are the ones with a verb base and a frequentative sense: craqueler (craquer) and the old cases in the TLFi (gratteler, panteler). Before writing 'verb + -eler', check that the base is a French verb or noun, that the sense is diminutive or frequentative, and that Wiktionary does not give a Latin etymon.

-iller.allomorphy: One form, -iller [i.je], added to a verb stem or noun stem (sauter → sautiller, mordre → mordiller, gosier → égosiller). The base's last letters change: sauter → saut-, mordre → mord-, fendre → fend-. fr.Wiktionary gives the learned equivalent -iculer (immatriculer, gesticuler).
-iller.origin_en: From Old French ~-ille~ or from Latin ~-iculare~; fr.Wiktionary offers both. en.Wiktionary had no French page for it.
-iller.origin_fr: De l'ancien français ~-ille~ ou du latin ~-iculare~ ; le wiktionnaire français propose les deux. Le wiktionnaire anglais n'a pas de page française.
senses: frequentative or diminutive: repeated small action (sautiller, mordiller, fendiller, pendiller)
pejorative or imprecise (bousiller, nasiller)
-iller.productive: The sources give no productivity rating, and the verbs cited are old; no recent coinage is attested in them.
cognates: Old Occitan -ilhar and Breton -ilhañ (fr.Wiktionary lists the Breton forms; en.Wiktionary compares Old Occitan fendilhar)
-iller.pitfalls: Most -iller verbs in the app are not 'base + -iller'. (1) Inherited from Latin: conseiller (Latin consiliare), mouiller (Vulgar Latin molliare), osciller (oscillare), distiller (distillare), vaciller (vacillare), titiller (titillare), surveiller and réveiller (from veiller, Latin vigilare). (2) Noun in -il, -ille or -eil + -er, so the -ill- belongs to the noun: fusiller (fusil), sommeiller (sommeil), ensoleiller (soleil), rouiller (rouille), fourmiller (fourmi). (3) Other bases: habiller, maquiller, gaspiller, brouiller, embrouiller, débrouiller, tortiller, éparpiller. Here -iller is not a clearly separate suffix and their origins vary or are uncertain, so check each. (4) Prefixed: déconseiller, déshabiller, agenouiller follow their base. Real derivations: sautiller (sauter), mordiller (mordre), fendiller (fendre; en.Wiktionary says possibly from Vulgar Latin *findiclāre instead), pendiller (pendre), égosiller (é- + gosier + -iller, from Old French esgosiller 'cut the throat'). bousiller: fr.Wiktionary says it comes from Occitan bosilhar; en.Wiktionary says bouse + -iller; the sources differ. nasiller is 'de nez' (fr), with a form that is not simple nez + -iller. Check: the base word is attested and the sense is a repeated or small action; otherwise it is an inherited word.

-ouiller.allomorphy: A single form. It is added to a verb or noun base after the base loses its ending (glander to glandouiller, pendre to pendouiller, vase to vasouiller). fr.Wiktionary says the suffix is -ouille plus the infinitive ending -er.
-ouiller.origin_en: Formed in French from ~-ouille~ and the verb ending ~-er~; fr.Wiktionary leaves the date unconfirmed.
-ouiller.origin_fr: Formé en français à partir de ~-ouille~ et de la terminaison verbale ~-er~ ; le Wiktionnaire ne confirme pas la date.
senses: diminutive or familiar: do X in a small, weak way (mâchouiller, crachouiller, pendouiller)
pejorative or idle action (glandouiller)
from a noun base (vasouiller, bafouiller, vadrouiller)
-ouiller.productive: A familiar, colloquial suffix. fr.Wiktionary lists many formations; the sources give no verdict beyond that.
cognates: none given in the sources; fr.Wiktionary lists Breton -ouilhañ as an equivalent
-ouiller.pitfalls: Most app verbs that end in -ouiller are not base + -ouiller. Many are formed on a root that already ends in -ouiller or -ouille: brouiller (débrouiller, embrouiller), rouiller (dérouiller), mouiller (remouiller), fouiller (refouiller, farfouiller, trifouiller), souiller, houille (déhouiller), grenouille (grenouiller), gargouille (gargouiller), verrou (verrouiller, déverrouiller), genou (agenouiller). dépouiller is inherited from Latin despoliare. fr.Wiktionary itself lists bafouiller, vadrouiller, bredouiller as suffix examples on nominal bases, but their bases are unclear to a learner; do not guess a base. gazouiller, chatouiller, gribouiller, patrouiller, barbouiller, bidouiller, magouiller, zigouiller, cafouiller: check; the sources do not settle them. Genuine verbal-base formations with the familiar nuance: glandouiller, pendouiller, mâchouiller, crachouiller, gratouiller, grattouiller (check). Before writing base + -ouiller, check that (a) a base verb or noun is present in the meaning (glander, pendre, vase), (b) the sense is diminutive or pejorative, (c) the verb is not on an -ouille noun or on mouiller/fouiller/brouiller/rouiller.

-iner.allomorphy: Single form -iner. The sources analyze it as a suffix on verbs (piéter + -iner) or as -in + -er; no allomorphs.
-iner.origin_en: The sources give no etymology for ~-iner~ itself. The evidence samples analyze it as a verb suffix (~piétiner~ from ~piéter~); it may be ~-in~ plus ~-er~, but this is unconfirmed.
-iner.origin_fr: Les sources ne donnent pas d'étymologie pour ~-iner~ lui-même. Les exemples l'analysent comme un suffixe verbal (~piétiner~ de ~piéter~) ; ce pourrait être ~-in~ plus ~-er~, mais rien ne le confirme.
senses: expressive or frequentative, repeated small action (piétiner 'stamp, keep stepping')
colloquial or slang flavor (enquiquiner, jaspiner)
-iner.productive: Not productive. Only a few colloquial, expressive verbs show it; piétiner is dated 1866 for the sense 'not advance'.
cognates: None established in the sources used
-iner.pitfalls: The great majority of app verbs ending in -iner are NOT formed with a suffix -iner. Groups: (1) Latin -inare verbs, borrowed or inherited: destiner, déterminer, terminer, imaginer, examiner, dominer, éliminer, décliner, combiner, deviner (divinare), contaminer, incliner, fasciner, illuminer, culminer, exterminer, disséminer, obstiner, prédominer, incriminer, confiner, entériner, dessiner (Latin designare via Italian). (2) Denominals from a noun already ending in -in(e): cuisiner (cuisine), assassiner (assassin), vacciner (vaccin), enraciner (racine), acheminer (chemin), cheminer, parrainer (parrain), avoisiner (voisin), mariner (marin, marine), peaufiner (peau + fin), affiner and raffiner (fin). (3) Other: freiner (frein), drainer (English drain). enquiquiner and jaspiner are in the input as -iner but their analyses are uncertain (kiki, japper). A writer must check whether the -in belongs to a noun or Latin root before using this card.

-onner.allomorphy: One form. The spelling is -onner with a double n; the older spelling -oner (téléphoner, and many verbs until the 18th century) has a single n and is a different ending (TLFi). Verbs from a noun in -on take a plain -er, which produces the same letters -onner (fonction + -er) without involving this suffix. The suffix itself is -on + -er, so it may appear as -on-er in analyses (chanter + -on + -er).
-onner.origin_en: According to the TLFi, ~-onner~ perhaps comes from the Latin frequentative suffixes ~-inare~ or ~-inire~; French Wiktionary analyses it as ~-on~ + ~-er~.
-onner.origin_fr: Selon le TLFi, ~-onner~ vient peut-être des suffixes fréquentatifs latins ~-inare~ ou ~-inire~ ; le Wiktionnaire français l'analyse comme ~-on~ + ~-er~.
senses: frequentative or diminutive on a verb: an action repeated or attenuated, often familiar (chantonner 'sing softly', mâchonner 'chew away', tâtonner)
dull continuous noise, on an onomatopoeic base (bougonner, ronchonner, marmonner, fredonner)
disorderly or pejorative action (fouillonner, brouillonner)
rarely on a noun (griffonner)
-onner.productive: Weak, in familiar register. The TLFi says -onner was rare until the 19th century and mainly formed verbs of a dull continuous noise, with some neologisms (grinçonner, goûtonner, fouillonner). Most new verbs in -onner today are not formed with this suffix.
cognates: No cognate affix is established by the sources consulted. The TLFi suggests the Latin frequentative suffixes -inare or -inire as a possible source.
-onner.pitfalls: This is the card with the largest false-positive set. Nearly every verb in the app that ends in -onner (and especially -ionner) is a noun in -on, -ion, -onne or -ond + the plain verb ending -er, and the TLFi names this as the homograph case (frissonner, couronner, plafonner). Examples: fonctionner (fonction), sélectionner, mentionner, passionner, positionner, sanctionner, raisonner, conditionner, soupçonner, fusionner, impressionner, occasionner, questionner, démissionner, façonner, couronner (couronne), plafonner (plafond), cantonner (canton), additionner, sillonner (sillon), rayonner (rayon), jalonner, actionner, visionner. Write 'noun + -er' for these, naming the noun. Other false positives: Latin descent (ordonner from ordinare, with the spelling of donner; pardonner from perdonare; résonner from resonare), prefix + donner (redonner, abandonner from a ban donner), randonner (Old French randonner, from randon), assaisonner (a- + saison + -er), empoisonner (en- + poison + -er). The true -onner verbs have a base verb or an onomatopoeic base and a frequentative or diminutive sense: chantonner (chanter), mâchonner (mâcher), tâtonner (tâter), griffonner (griffer), plus fredonner, bougonner, marmonner. Before writing 'verb + -onner', check that a French verb (or an imitative base) precedes -onner and that the sense is 'softly, repeatedly, aimlessly'. If a noun in -on or -ion precedes -ner, say 'noun + -er'.

-ocher.allomorphy: One form, -ocher, added to a noun or verb stem (boule → boulocher, flâner → flânocher). It is described as 'from -oche + -er'.
-ocher.origin_en: Formed in French from the suffix ~-oche~ and the verbal ending ~-er~.
-ocher.origin_fr: Formé en français à partir du suffixe ~-oche~ et de la terminaison verbale ~-er~.
senses: pejorative or familiar: do poorly or in a petty way (flânocher, boulocher 'form small balls, pill')
popular register with deprecatory value (balocher, pétocher)
-ocher.productive: Only a few verbs, informal in register; fr.Wiktionary calls it a 'popular suffix with deprecatory value'. It is not used to coin new verbs in general.
cognates: No cognate in other languages was found beyond Breton -ochañ (fr.Wiktionary); no cognate is claimed
-ocher.pitfalls: Almost all the app verbs ending in -ocher are not derived with this suffix. In accrocher, décrocher, raccrocher (croc), empocher, rempocher (poche), embrocher, débrocher (broche), décocher, encocher (coche), enrocher, dérocher (roc), talocher (taloche), the -och- is part of the base noun and the ending is just -er. approcher, rapprocher and reprocher come from Latin-derived bases, not from -ocher. ricocher is from ricochet. guillocher is from guilloche. Treat any verb as -ocher only when the sources say so and the base noun or verb (without -och-) exists: boulocher (boule + -oche + -er per en.Wiktionary; fr.Wiktionary has it as 'dérivé de boule, avec le suffixe -ocher', the two differ on whether -oche is a separate step). rabibocher is listed by fr.Wiktionary as an -ocher word, but its base is unclear, so avoid analysing it. The others listed (balocher, flânocher, garrocher, mignocher, pétocher) are from fr.Wiktionary's examples.

-âcher.allomorphy: A single form; the circumflex marks an old lost s (rabascher became rabâcher, per fr.Wiktionary).
-âcher.origin_en: Of unclear origin. fr.Wiktionary analyses ~rabâcher~ as the radical ~rab-~ plus ~-âcher~, from Old French ~rabascher~; en.Wiktionary derives it from a root *~rabb-~, possibly from a substrate.
-âcher.origin_fr: D'origine incertaine. Le Wiktionnaire français analyse ~rabâcher~ comme le radical ~rab-~ plus ~-âcher~, issu de l'ancien français ~rabascher~ ; le Wiktionnaire anglais le dérive d'une racine *~rabb-~, peut-être d'un substrat.
senses: frequentative or noisy repeated action (rabâcher: 'say the same things again and again')
-âcher.productive: Not productive. Only rabâcher is in the data, and it is not a clean 'base + suffix' case.
cognates: none given in the sources
-âcher.pitfalls: Do not write 'base + -âcher' for any verb. Even for rabâcher the sources disagree: fr.Wiktionary sees a radical rab- (compare rabouin 'devil, goblin') plus the suffix, en.Wiktionary a root *rabb- that may come from a substrate, and Old French had rabaster 'make noise'. relâcher is inherited from Latin relaxare, so it contains no suffix; remâcher is re- + mâcher (see the re- card), and the -âcher is part of mâcher. Other verbs in -âcher (lâcher, tâcher, fâcher) are not formed with this suffix. A writer who has only the verb rabâcher should say 'of uncertain origin' and give both proposals.

-in.allomorphy: Single form -in, feminine -ine. It is a noun and adjective suffix, not a verb-forming suffix. A verb in -iner can contain it plus the verbal -er.
senses: diminutive or pejorative (oursin, plaisantin)
belonging or relation (marin, périgordin)
for ratatiner: -in as a diminutive on tatin 'small amount', per fr.Wiktionary
-in.productive: Productive for demonyms and some nouns; not a verb-forming suffix.
cognates: Latin -īnus (source)
-in.pitfalls: ratatiner has a disputed origin: fr.Wiktionary gives ra- + tatin ('small amount', itself tant + diminutive -in), and en.Wiktionary says onomatopoeic. Say 'uncertain' rather than choosing. The suffix -in is NOT a verb suffix; a verb in -iner is not evidence of -in. For verbs ending in -iner see the -iner card. Do not use this card for destiner, déterminer, etc.

-type.allomorphy: One form. It is a noun-forming element, so a verb in -typer is the noun in -type plus the verb ending -er, not a verb suffix. There is no shape change.
-type.origin_en: From Ancient Greek ~τύπος~ (~túpos~, “mark, impression”), the source of French ~type~. French Wiktionary treats ~-type~ as forming nouns about imprints (printing, photography, genetics).
-type.origin_fr: Du grec ancien ~τύπος~ (~túpos~, « empreinte, marque »), d'où le français ~type~. Le Wiktionnaire français décrit ~-type~ comme formant des substantifs relatifs aux empreintes (imprimerie, photographie, génétique).
senses: forms nouns for an imprint, print or reproduction (ronéotype; photographic and printing terms)
in the verb ronéotyper, 'to reproduce on a Roneo duplicator' (fr.Wiktionary: composé de ronéo, avec le suffixe -type)
-type.productive: Productive for scientific and technical nouns; for verbs, hardly at all. The sources give no productivity rating. The only app verb here, ronéotyper, names an obsolete duplicating machine.
cognates: English -type (from Ancient Greek tupos, 'mark, type')
Greek tupos, the direct source
-type.pitfalls: Do not call -type a verb-forming suffix. The sources show -type as a noun-forming element (ronéotype, ronéotypie), so ronéotyper is best explained as built on the noun ronéotype (itself from Ronéo, a trademark from English Roneo, 1901, and type) plus the verb ending -er; fr.Wiktionary's wording 'ronéo + suffixe -type' is shorter but loose. State the trademark origin (Roneo, a portmanteau of rotary and neo-). The synonym ronéoter is ronéo + -er. No other verb in the app ends in -type. If a writer meets another verb ending in -typer, check whether the base is a noun in -type; do not assume a prefix-and-suffix pattern.
